title: Immunisation & occupational health
blurb: Hepatitis B vaccination and why your response is checked, what sero-conversion means, and reporting skin problems and illness to protect yourself and patients.
question: A new trainee has just finished her hepatitis B injections and assumes she is now protected. A month later her hands are red and cracked from gloves, and one morning she wakes with a chesty cough when the practice is short-staffed. What should she do in each situation?

teach.h: Protecting the person behind the PPE
teach.body: Every day you handle instruments covered in saliva and blood, so you are at risk of blood-borne viruses. Immunisation removes the 'susceptible host' link in the chain of infection. Hepatitis B immunisation is recommended for all clinical staff who may come into contact with blood or blood-stained saliva, and HTM 01-05 expects staff in decontamination to show current hepatitis B immunisation. Your employer arranges it, usually through occupational health, and keeps a record of your immune status.

root.label: Course of hepatitis B vaccine
root.sub: Usually three doses over several months

children.label: Responder
children.sub: Protected; result recorded by occupational health

children.label: Non-responder
children.sub: Occupational health advises on further doses and on urgent action after any exposure

teach.caption: Finishing the course is not proof of protection. Only the antibody blood test shows whether the vaccine worked.

teach.body: Sero-conversion is the point at which antibodies to a particular virus or vaccine can be detected in the blood. After hepatitis B vaccination, sero-conversion is good news: it shows your immune system has responded. After a sharps injury from an infected patient, sero-conversion to that virus means you have been infected. That's why occupational health may arrange follow-up blood tests for several months after an inoculation injury.

head: Infection
Why it matters in dentistry
rows: Blood-borne; vaccine plus antibody check for clinical staff
Wounds from contaminated instruments; subject to local policy
Spread by air; dangerous to pregnant and vulnerable patients
Airborne; status checked when you start
Vaccine offered yearly to protect you and patients
teach.caption: There is no vaccine for hepatitis C or HIV, so safe sharps practice and PPE are your only protection against them.

teach.h: What occupational health does for you
teach.body: Occupational health is a confidential service that looks after your health at work. It checks your immunity when you start, gives vaccines and keeps records, manages follow-up after sharps and splash injuries, and assesses work-related problems such as skin conditions or latex allergy. Dental nurses don't carry out exposure-prone procedures, so they don't routinely need the extra health clearance that dentists need. Looking after your own health and asking for advice early is part of your professional duty.

rows.label: Cause
values: Frequent washing, wet work, glove wear
Immune reaction, e.g. to glove chemicals or latex

rows.label: Looks like
values: Itchy rash where the trigger touches

teach.caption: Cracked skin is a portal of entry for infection. Occupational dermatitis diagnosed by a doctor can be reportable under RIDDOR.

steps.label: Notice your symptoms
steps.sub: e.g. respiratory infection, diarrhoea and vomiting

steps.label: Follow the illness policy
steps.sub: Even if the practice is short-staffed

steps.label: Return when the policy allows
steps.sub: Often 48 hours symptom-free after D and V

teach.text: Completing a hepatitis B course does not mean you are protected: some people don't respond. Your antibody level must be checked and recorded. And 'we're short-staffed' is never a reason to ignore the illness policy.

items: Hepatitis B immunisation is recommended for all clinical staff, with a blood test to confirm response.
Sero-conversion means antibodies have appeared: good after vaccination, infection after exposure.
There is no vaccine for hepatitis C or HIV.
Report dry, cracked or itchy hands to occupational health early.
Follow the practice illness policy when unwell, even when short-staffed.

summary: You can now explain why hepatitis B immunisation is needed and why your response is checked, define sero-conversion in both its meanings, describe what occupational health does, and act correctly on hand dermatitis and illness.

A.q: A trainee dental nurse who assists with surgical extractions asks which immunisation is most relevant to her role. What is the best answer?
A.why: Clinical staff exposed to blood should be immunised against hepatitis B and have their response confirmed by a blood test.

whyNot.0: Yellow fever is a travel vaccine with no link to dental work.
whyNot.2: Flu vaccine is offered, but it doesn't protect against blood-borne viruses.
whyNot.3: Hepatitis A spreads mainly through contaminated food and water, not blood in the surgery.

A.q: A nurse finishes her hepatitis B course and asks whether she is now protected. Why is her response checked with a blood test?
options: The vaccine expires after a month
It confirms she has not been infected
Some people do not respond to it
The test replaces the final dose
A.why: A proportion of people don't produce protective antibodies, so response is checked rather than assumed.

whyNot.0: Protection doesn't expire after a month.
whyNot.1: The test checks for antibodies made in response to the vaccine.
whyNot.3: The test is done after the course; it doesn't replace a dose.

A.q: After months of frequent glove use, a nurse's hands are red, dry and cracked. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Wear two pairs of gloves to protect the skin
A.why: Work-related skin problems should be reported early so occupational health can assess the cause and advise.

whyNot.1: Double gloving doesn't treat the skin and may make it worse.
whyNot.2: Alcohol rub on cracked skin can sting and dry it further; it doesn't solve the problem.
whyNot.3: Hand hygiene is still essential; the skin problem needs assessment.

B.q: What does the term sero-conversion mean?
options: Converting a vaccine into a booster dose
B.why: Sero-conversion is when antibodies to a virus or vaccine become detectable in the blood.

whyNot.0: Changing glove type is unrelated to sero-conversion.
whyNot.1: Changing duties is a work arrangement, not a blood result.
whyNot.2: Boosters are extra doses; sero-conversion describes the body's response.

B.q: A dental nurse wakes with a respiratory infection and the practice is short-staffed. What should she do?
options: Follow the illness policy and get advice
Come in and wear an extra mask
Work but avoid talking to patients
Take paracetamol and work as usual
B.why: Illness should be reported and the practice policy followed, so infection isn't passed to patients and colleagues.

whyNot.1: An extra mask doesn't remove the risk of spreading infection.
whyNot.2: Avoiding conversation doesn't stop transmission by droplets and contact.
whyNot.3: Masking symptoms with medication still leaves her infectious.

B.q: Which of these is a role of occupational health?
B.why: Occupational health manages staff after inoculation injuries, including risk assessment, treatment and follow-up.

whyNot.0: Autoclave validation is done by engineers and competent persons.
whyNot.1: Occupational health looks after staff, not patients.
whyNot.3: Prescribing for patients is the dentist's role.

C.q: A nurse is found to be a non-responder after her hepatitis B course. What does this mean?
options: Her blood shows no protective antibodies
She can never again work in clinical areas
C.why: A non-responder hasn't produced protective antibodies, so occupational health advises on further doses and on what to do after any exposure.

whyNot.0: Non-response means no vaccine antibodies, not infection.
whyNot.3: She can work with advice from occupational health and careful practice.

C.q: A nurse develops an itchy rash wherever her latex gloves touch her skin. What should happen?
C.why: This could be an allergy, so it should be reported and assessed by occupational health; latex-free gloves may be needed.

whyNot.0: Continuing exposure to an allergen can make the reaction worse.
whyNot.2: Hand cream doesn't stop an allergic reaction and may affect gloves.
whyNot.3: Cotton gloves are not a clinical barrier.

C.q: After a needlestick from a patient with hepatitis C, why might occupational health arrange blood tests over the following months?
options: To check her vaccine is up to date
C.why: Follow-up tests look for sero-conversion, which would show she had been infected and needs treatment.

whyNot.0: There is no vaccine for hepatitis C.
whyNot.1: The injury is recorded in the accident book; blood tests are for her health.
whyNot.2: Iron levels are unrelated to the exposure.

reteach.title: A lock you have to test
reteach.question: If you fitted a new lock on your door, you'd turn the key to check it works. Why is hepatitis B vaccination the same?

blocks.h: Fit the lock, then test it
blocks.body: The vaccine course is like fitting a lock, and the antibody blood test is turning the key to check it. For most people the lock works and the result goes on your record. For some it doesn't, and you need to know, because you'd act differently after a sharps injury. Occupational health is the locksmith: it fits, tests and keeps the records, and it helps when something goes wrong, whether that is an injury, sore hands or an illness.

blocks.text: Sero-conversion after vaccination = protected. Sero-conversion after exposure to an infected patient = infected.

explain.body: Recommended for all clinical staff exposed to blood. A course of injections is followed by a blood test, because some people don't respond. Occupational health records the result.

test.q: What confirms that a nurse has responded to hepatitis B vaccine?
options: Antibody level in a blood test
A red mark at the injection site
test.why: A blood test measures antibodies to hepatitis B to confirm the vaccine has worked.

whyNot.3: A saliva swab doesn't measure vaccine response.

explain.body: The appearance of antibodies in the blood. After vaccination, it shows protection. After exposure to an infected patient, it shows infection, which is why staff are followed up after inoculation injuries.

test.q: After a needlestick from an HIV-positive patient, a nurse's later blood test shows sero-conversion. What does this mean?
test.why: Sero-conversion to HIV after an exposure means antibodies to the virus are present, so she has been infected.

whyNot.0: Sero-conversion after exposure indicates infection, not harmlessness.
whyNot.2: If PEP had worked, she would not sero-convert.

explain.body: Frequent washing and gloves can cause irritant dermatitis; some people develop allergies to glove chemicals or latex. Dry hands well, use emollient, and report problems early to occupational health.

test.q: Which helps prevent irritant hand dermatitis?
options: Using alcohol rub on wet hands
test.why: Drying hands thoroughly and using emollient cream protects the skin barrier.

whyNot.0: Longer glove wear traps moisture and irritates skin.
whyNot.2: Hot water strips natural oils and dries skin.
whyNot.3: Alcohol rub belongs on dry hands; on wet hands it works poorly.

explain.body: Tell your manager before your shift and follow the illness policy, even when the practice is busy or short-staffed. Seek advice when you need it, and return only when the policy allows.

test.q: A nurse had diarrhoea and vomiting overnight but feels better by morning. What should she do?
options: Come in, as symptoms have stopped
Report it and follow the policy
test.why: She may still be infectious, so she should report it and follow the illness policy, which usually sets a symptom-free period.

whyNot.0: People can remain infectious after symptoms stop.
whyNot.1: Reception still involves contact with patients and colleagues.
whyNot.3: Medication hides symptoms but doesn't stop her being infectious.
